https://www.chicagotribune.com/2026/10/1.text: By Jonathan Bullington | jbullington@chicagotribune.com | Chicago Tribune PUBLISHED: October 18, 2026 at 5:00 AM CDT Annie Girresch, center, receives a kiss from her mentor, Elsie McGrath, on the day Girresch joined McGrath as an ordained Catholic priest. The ceremony was held at St. John’s United Church of Christ in St. Louis on June 27, 2026. (Eileen T. Meslar/Chicago Tribune) Getting your Trinity Audio player ready... ST. LOUIS — The entire day had been building to this moment. First there was the procession, then the readings and songs and the sponsors who explained why they felt she was ready for what was to come. She prostrated before the altar inside the old church, her chest heaving with emotion as the Litany of the Saints was said. She sat in a folding chair, tears trickling down her cheeks, while each person in the pews came forward to place their hands on her head in a quiet blessing. And as the noon hour arrived and Anna Girresch — Annie to those who know her — held out her hands to be anointed with oil, it felt like all 70-plus people in attendance collectively held their breaths as the ritual neared its culmination. It came seconds later, when a bishop raised Annie’s right hand toward the ceiling and, “with great joy,” introduced her as a newly ordained Catholic priest. The congregation — Annie’s parents and sisters, nephews and friends and 12 other women whose ranks she joined that last Saturday in June — stood and cheered for a full minute. No one seemed bothered that they had just been willing participants in a ceremony the Roman Catholic Church deems a grave sin, or that Annie had just incurred one of its most severe punishments: automatic and immediate excommunication. Ellen Girresch, center, and her husband, Wil, clap as their daughter Annie Girresch speaks at the end of her ordination Mass held June 27 at a St. Louis church. (Eileen T. Meslar/Chicago Tribune) “I’m just filled with the spirit right now and so blessed that she’s going to go forth and share God with all the people that she touches,” her father, Wil Girresch, said between thanking people who stopped to congratulate him. “This is what the church needs to be,” added his wife, Ellen Girresch. “Accepting. Supporting.” Annie is the latest in a line of women, some 300 in all, scattered across the United States and in at least nine other countries, who in the last two decades have defied the Catholic Church to be ordained as deacons, priests and bishops. These women — cradle Catholics and converts, former nuns, teachers, hospice chaplains, counselors, spouses, mothers, grandmothers — say their defiance is the fulfillment of a vocation, no different than the call answered by their male counterparts. Most have advanced degrees in theology or divinity that prepared them, they say, to serve. Already, over Catholicism’s roughly 2,000-year history, women have become saints who founded missions and religious orders. They have taught theology in schools and prepared young men for the priesthood. They’ve run hospitals and universities. In Chicago, the archdiocese’s chief operating officer is a woman. So, too, is the CEO of Catholic Charities. But the church has always barred women from becoming priests and bishops, a rule it traces to Jesus’ choice of apostles. In 1983, the Vatican codified its position with canon law 1024 , which reads: “A baptized male alone receives sacred ordination validly.” Women choosing to break that law have been called exiles, a rogue schismatic group akin to the recently excommunicated Society of St. Pius X , even a cult. But the priests do not see it that way. “We don’t stand at midnight in the moonlight swinging dead cats around,” said Mary Keldermans, a Springfield native who was ordained a priest in 2014 and a bishop in 2021. “People think we made up our church. It’s not true. We’re Catholic.” Keldermans and others acknowledge it is unlikely that Chicago-born Pope Leo XIV , whom they generally like, will shift the church’s position. Still, as they watch the faith struggle with shrinking congregations, shuttered schools and the damage done by abusive male clergy , most are hopeful their efforts will eventually open the door to women in the priesthood — and in doing so, transform an institution they see as having excluded too many for too long. “I think what will happen is there will be so many of us,” said Eileen Mathy of Urbana, ordained in 2023, “that at one point the church will say, ‘What were we so afraid of?’” Bishop Martha Mary Sherman, left, raises Annie Girresch's right hand toward the ceiling and, “with great joy,” introduces her as a newly ordained Catholic priest on June 27, 2026. (Eileen T. Meslar/Chicago Tribune) Jem Ward, 3, left, waits in line behind his cousin Noah Bachmann, 8, as Noah lays his hands on the head of his aunt, Annie Girresch, at Girresch’s ordination Mass on June 27, 2026. (Eileen T. Meslar/Chicago Tribune) Bishop Martha Mary Sherman, right, celebrates Mass with newly ordained priest Annie Girresch, center, on June 27, 2026. (Eileen T. Meslar/Chicago Tribune) Annie Girresch, center, sings with other priests during her ordination Mass at St. John’s United Church of Christ in St. Louis on June 27, 2026. (Eileen T. Meslar/Chicago Tribune) Tina Thompson, an ordained priest, lays her hands on the head of Annie Girresch during Girresch’s ordination Mass at St. John’s United Church of Christ on June 27, 2026. (Eileen T. Meslar/Chicago Tribune) Female priests hug one another during the ordination Mass for Annie Girresch at St. John’s United Church of Christ on June 27, 2026. (Eileen T. Meslar/Chicago Tribune) Mary Kay Kusner, left, fixes Annie Girresch’s chasuble at Girresch’s ordination at St. John’s United Church of Christ. (Eileen T. Meslar/Chicago Tribune) Members of the Roman Catholic Womenpriests organization wait for the ordination of Annie Girresch to begin at St. John’s United Church of Christ in St. Louis on June 27, 2026. (Eileen T. Meslar/Chicago Tribune) Linda Wilcox, left, an ordained priest, hugs Annie Girresch on the morning of Girresch’s ordination. (Eileen T. Meslar/Chicago Tribune) Show Caption 1 of 9 Bishop Martha Mary Sherman, left, raises Annie Girresch's right hand toward the ceiling and, “with great joy,” introduces her as a newly ordained Catholic priest on June 27, 2026. (Eileen T. Meslar/Chicago Tribune) Expand In the meantime, female priests have built communities that worship in living rooms, rented storefronts, churches borrowed from other Christian faiths or on Zoom. Their services often draw people who also feel marginalized or rejected by an institution whose positions on topics like sexual orientation or divorce they can no longer abide. “I see (women priests) as a bridge, creating a place for people who cannot find themselves or pray in a traditional male clerical church,” said Jean Marchant, a Massachusetts native who was ordained a priest in 2005 and a bishop in 2019. “We’re creating a home for them, a place for them to pray together and live their lives out of that faithfulness.” It’s easy to question why these women don’t decide instead to convert to a faith that allows female pastors. Indeed, they have paid a steep price in pursuit of the priesthood. Beyond adding their names to an excommunication list that includes St. Joan of Arc, Martin Luther and Fidel Castro, some have resigned from or been forced to leave jobs or volunteer positions in their dioceses. Some have incurred criticism from loved ones and threats from strangers. One Chicago priest dying from cancer was denied a funeral mass at her longtime parish. But the women say the priesthood is not a choice they made. It’s a calling. They were pulled to it, often reluctantly, led by an unseen hand down a path they realized they had been seeking much of their lives. Susan Vaickauski celebrates a Catholic Mass with her congregation at Northbrook United Methodist Church on Sept. 19, 2026. (Eileen T. Meslar/Chicago Tribune) Susan Vaickauski, second from right, prays with her congregants at the altar during Mass at Northbrook United Methodist Church on June 20, 2026. (Eileen T. Meslar/Chicago Tribune) Susan Vaickauski blesses her congregation as she celebrates Mass at Northbrook United Methodist Church on June 20, 2026. (Eileen T. Meslar/Chicago Tribune) Steve Forst, clockwise from top, Donna Birren, Jim Allen and Julie Bennett Lefkow laugh as they catch up before Mass at a Methodist church in Northbrook on June 20, 2026. (Eileen T. Meslar/Chicago Tribune) Show Caption 1 of 4 Susan Vaickauski celebrates a Catholic Mass with her congregation at Northbrook United Methodist Church on Sept. 19, 2026. (Eileen T. Meslar/Chicago Tribune) Expand “You know, when you fight something you know you’re supposed to do, it’s painful,” said Susan Vaickauski, who was ordained in 2016 and pastors a congregation in Northbrook. “It’s the unknown. ‘How’s it going to work? Who’s going to be affected? How are they going to be affected?’ But when God calls you, no is not an alternative, because God is going to keep after you until you say yes.” The call On days when they weren’t outside helping care for the dairy cows and pigs and chickens, or preparing vegetables to be canned and stored in the cellar, Katherine Elsner and her seven siblings played Mass. Their chapel was typically the living room inside their one-story farmhouse in Greensburg, Indiana, 50 miles southeast of that state’s capital. A small table served as the altar, Necco Wafers as the Communion host. Elsner, while not the eldest of the kids, always assumed the role of priest. Other female priests tell similar stories of childhoods spent deeply connected to Catholicism. For Angela Nevitt Meyer, ordained in 2021, that meant hours spent in her bedroom imagining conversations with Jesus’ mother, Mary, or reading about the lives of saints instead of playing with her younger brother and the other kids in their neighborhood outside Peoria. Girresch was in the music ministry at her parish in suburban St. Louis. Vaickauski demonstrated such devoutness at her Catholic grade school in Lafayette, Indiana, that a nun selected her in seventh and eighth grade to help prepare for each morning’s Mass. Katherine Elsner sings while attending a Mass celebrated by Mary Keldermans on Aug. 8, 2026, at Holy Family Inclusive Catholic Community in Springfield, where Elsner is also a member of the clergy. (Eileen T. Meslar/Chicago Tribune) With that faith, though, came moments when they questioned why the church they loved seemed to treat them differently. Long before she was ordained in 2021, Elsner joined a convent in Springfield run by Dominican sisters — in part, she said, because it was “a way for me to be somebody in the church.” She spent three decades as a teacher and principal at Catholic schools in Illinois, then another 16 as her order’s treasurer. Though life as a Dominican had been rewarding, she wanted more independence. Ten years into her time as treasurer she left the convent, though she remained in the position another six years as a laywoman. Prior to becoming treasurer, while studying finance at the University of Notre Dame, she devoured books by female theologians and started to ask herself why women couldn’t be deacons and priests in the Catholic Church. “It didn’t make sense,” she said. “Why were women excluded? Nobody really asked that question out loud too much, and especially in my community, which tended to be more conservative than some other orders. I knew I couldn’t ask that question out loud.” Katherine Elsner, center, holds the hand of Mary Kay Kusner, also an ordained priest, before Annie Girresch's ordination Mass in June. (Eileen T. Meslar/Chicago Tribune) Now she was free to do that. One day in 2016, she and a friend saw an advertisement in a Springfield newspaper for the Catholic church pastored by Mary Keldermans. Her friend turned to her and said, “Let’s go see what this woman priest is like.” From that first visit, Elsner became a regular at Keldermans’ church. The two women talked often, and their conversations eventually drifted to the priesthood. The prospect frightened Elsner, at first. “I was doing something against the church that I had been faithful to for 70 years,” she said. And yet, she added, “I just knew it was something I needed to do, for myself as well as an example for any other women who are afraid.” The Danube Seven Before Anna Girresch, before Katherine Elsner and Jean Marchant and Susan Vaickauski and the rest, there were the Danube Seven. One June morning in 2002, on a day when Catholics celebrate the feasts of Sts. Peter and Paul, around 250 people boarded the MS Passau, a boat built to carry passengers on scenic day cruises along the Danube River between Germany and Austria. They came to see seven women become priests. By the time they disembarked that day, a movement had taken shape. The theological and historical debate over women in the priesthood is nuanced and complex. On one side is a Vatican that says, in part, that it has no authority to ordain women because Jesus chose only men to be his apostles and because men, alone, can represent his image. Proponents of female priests argue that the earliest Christians prayed and broke bread in homes where women, as hosts, would have presided over those gatherings. Adding fuel to the debate is the discovery of ancient artifacts — texts, frescoes, tombstone inscriptions — that seem, to some, to depict women as priests in the early Catholic Church. “People who look at the early church argue it’s not surprising that we see women in these prominent roles because many women in antiquities were civic leaders,” said Haley Bowen, an assistant professor in Northwestern University’s history department. “Countering that we have a number of Gospel texts and other schools within the early church that are very much opposed to women’s participation in priestly functions.” Seven women are ordained as Catholic priests aboard a boat on the Danube River on June 29, 2009. The women, known as "the Danube Seven," were excommunicated by the Vatican. (Roman Catholic Womenpriests) The Vatican sought to settle the matter in 1976, when it issued a declaration , approved by Pope Paul VI, stating in part “that the Church, in fidelity to the example of the Lord, does not consider herself authorized to admit women to priestly ordination. … It is a position which will perhaps cause pain but whose positive value will become apparent in the long run, since it can be of help in deepening understanding of the respective roles of men and of women.” Still, exceptions have been made. Perhaps most notably, in 1970, amid the persecution of Catholics in Communist-controlled Czechoslovakia, the underground church there needed priests. Bishop Felix Davidek responded by secretly ordaining married men and some women, including Ludmila Javorová. Javorová kept her secret from the broader public for much of the next two decades, through the fall of her country’s Communist government. Finally, the Vatican ordered her to end her ministry in 1996. She died last month at 94. Thirty-two years after her ordination, the seven women ordained aboard the MS Passau included four from Germany, two from Austria and one from the United States, a former first lady of Ohio, no less. They chose the boat to avoid disruptions from protesters or church officials. Romulo Antonio Braschi, a male Catholic bishop, and a second man he had ordained as a bishop, performed the ordinations. A third bishop had been invited but did not show up. Conflicting accounts from those in attendance say he was either held up by traffic or held against his will by male priests, friends of his, who locked him in his room to prevent him from attending. A little over a month later, the Vatican issued a decree of excommunication to the women, who became known as “the Danube Seven.” It stated that Braschi had previously been excommunicated “as a schisma
